fields.label: Title of the dataset
fields.text: Crops and Livestock Products

fields.label: Source organisation
fields.text: FAOSTAT

fields.label: Data processing
fields.text: Aggregate item codes are removed prior to analysis to prevent double counting, as FAOSTAT includes both component crops and their rolled-up totals (e.g. Cereals primary, Fruit Primary). Following the FAO methodology, total crop yield is computed as the sum of production across all crop items divided by the total harvested area, expressed in kg/ha. Similarly, total livestock yield are computed as the sum of production across all retained livestock items dividedby the total number of producting animals, expressed in kg/animal.

fields.label: License
fields.text: CC BY 4.0

fields.label: Additional comments
fields.text:
Example: 
 In 2002, Tonga reported a crop yield of 6114 kilograms per hectare. By 2022, this value had increased to 7325 kilograms per hectare, indicating a rise in crop yields over the period. 
 In 1962, Kiribati recorded an area-weighted average livestock yield of 1 460 kg per animal across all retained livestock items. By 2024, this value had increased to 2 508 kg per animal, indicating a rise in livestock productivity over the period.

fields.label: Comment
fields.text: Data are sourced directly from NSO websites and compiled manually into a regional dataset.

fields.label: Data processing
fields.text: Consumer Price Indices (CPI) are compiled in accordance with international standards, namely the Consumer Price Index Manual (2020 or 2004 version). Specific information on national CPI compilation practices is available from the IMF Dissemination Standards Bulletin Board (DSBB): https://dsbb.imf.org/ (https://dsbb.imf.org/) The conceptual basis of a CPI is to measure the rate at which prices of consumption goods and services change over time. The annual average inflation rate is calculated as the percentage change between the average CPI index for a calendar year and the corresponding average CPI index for the previous calendar year. Minor variations or discrepancies in percentage changes and aggregate sums may reflect rounding differences.

fields.label: Revision policy
fields.text: Revisions made by National Statistics Offices (NSOs) after data have been compiled may not be reflected immediately in this regional dataset. Users requiring the latest official figures should refer to the relevant NSO.

fields.label: Additional comments
fields.text: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the prices of a representative basket of goods and services purchased by a typical household and is a commonly used measure of inflation. The basket is weighted to reflect typical spending patterns and is updated periodically to account for changes in consumption habits. Annual average inflation differs from year-on-year inflation, which compares a specific month (or quarter) with the corresponding period of the previous year. Because annual average inflation is based on the average of all monthly (or quarterly) index observations within a calendar year, it tends to be less volatile and smooths short-term fluctuations in prices.

fields.label: Source organisation
fields.text: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

fields.label: Comment
fields.text: Monthly and yearly currency exchange rates are collected from IMF International Financial Statistics, using the SDMX API. Exchange rates are domestic currency per U.S. Dollar for currencies used by Pacific Island Countries and Territories : Australian Dollar, CFP Franc, Fiji Dollar, Kina, New Zealand Dollar, Pa’anga, Solomon Islands Dollar, Tala and Vatu. End of period rates and period average rates are collected. The call to IMF API used to collect the data is: http://dataservices.imf.org/REST/SDMX_XML.svc/CompactData/IFS/A+M.FJ+NC+PG+SB+TO+VU+WS+AU+NZ.ENDA_XDC_USD_RATE+ENDE_XD C_USD_RATE?startPeriod=1950&endPeriod=2050 (http://dataservices.imf.org/REST/SDMX_XML.svc/CompactData/IFS/A+M.FJ+NC+PG+SB+TO+VU+WS+AU+NZ.ENDA_XDC_USD_RATE+ENDE_XDC_USD_RATE?startPeriod=1950&endPeriod=2050)

fields.label: Data processing
fields.text: Data values are rounded to 4 decimal places. Quarterly values are calculated from monthly values: end of perdiod value of the last month of the quarter is used for end of period rate, average of average monthly rates is used for period average rate. Reference area ISO3166-1 alpha 2 codes are recoded to ISO 4217 currency codes this way: FJ-FJD, NC-XPF, PG-PGK, SB-SBD, TO-TOP, VU-VUV, WS-WST, AU-AUD, NZ-NZD.

fields.label: Revision policy
fields.text: The full dataset is reloaded from IMF at the beginning of each month, but historical data is in principle not revised.

fields.label: Source organisation

fields.label: Data processing
fields.text: The raw dataset contains values expressed in both domestic currency and as a percentage of GDP. Only observations expressed as "Percent of GDP" are retained. The indicator is disaggregated by tax type (Energy, Transport, Pollution, Resources, and total Environmental Taxes). Tax category labels are simplified by removing redundant prefixes and standardizing nomenclature.

fields.label: License
fields.text: International Monetary Fund Copyright. All Rights Reserved.

fields.label: Additional comments
fields.text: Data are sourced from IMF Climate Change Dashboard, which itself sources from OECD. Coverage is extremely limited for Pacific Island countries, with only 5 SPC member countries reporting data (overall missing rate: 43.8%). The total environmental taxes value is computed only when all disaggregated categories (Energy, Transport, Pollution, Resources) are documented for a given country-year. \n Example: \n In 2011, Fiji recorded a value of 0.89, indicating that 0.89% of Fiji’s GDP was from environmental taxes at that time. By 2020, the indicator for Fiji was 0.4, meaning that 0.4% of Fiji’s GDP was from environmental taxes.

fields.text: Meteorological monitoring network

fields.label: Source organisation
fields.text: WMO - OSCAR Database

fields.label: Data processing
fields.text: Only stations classified as operational are retained; stations with "Silent" or "Unknown" reporting status are excluded. Years of operation are extracted from establishment and closure dates. When closure date is missing and the station is assessed as operational, the current year is used as the end date. For each station, the indicator increments by 1 for each year between establishment and closure (or present if still active). The indicator is calculated both as a total count and disaggregated by station type.

fields.label: License
fields.text: CC BY-SA 4.0

fields.label: Additional comments
fields.text: Data are sourced from WMO's OSCAR database. The conservative filtering approach (excluding non-operational stations) may underestimate the total number of monitoring stations but ensures data robustness. The indicator is disaggregated by station type to allow differentiation between various meteorological monitoring capabilities. \n Example : \n In 1889, Samoa recorded a value of 1, indicating that one meteorological station was in place at that time. By 2025, the indicator for Samoa had reached 4, meaning that 4 stations were in place.

fields.label: Title of the dataset
fields.text: Administrative data collected from customs ASYCUDAWorld application. Data is exchanged between national customs authorities and the Pacific Community under a specific Data Licence Agreement (DLA).

fields.label: Data processing
fields.text: Commodity trade data processed by the Statistics for Development Division (SDD) of the Pacific Community (SPC) and published on the Pacific Data Hub .Stat statistical database under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Public License (CC-BY-4.0) (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/legalcode). The PACComtrade datasets are administrative statistics automatically generated from customs data. These datasets are updated monthly through an automated process. The system applies a series of validation rules to ensure data quality, including checks for the presence of mandatory fields and the validity of classification codes (e.g. country or commodity codes). Each time the process is executed, a validation report is produced, summarising any inconsistencies or erroneous entries. This report is shared with the relevant customs organisation for review and correction, if necessary. Technical documentation of the PACComtrade process can be found on the dedicated GitHub repository (https://github.com/PacificCommunity/PACComtrade).

fields.label: Additional comments
fields.text:
The following caveats with respect to the exhaustiveness applies to the PACComtrade database:
 
 PACComtrade database is a commodity trade database and not International Merchandise Trade Statistics (IMTS) i.e., these data sourced from Customs Administrations are used for compiling IMTS by National Statistics Offices (NSO) but are supplemented with data from other sources as well. For example, fuel sold to visiting aircraft, which is re-export, are not captured by quite a number of Customs administrations so the NSO’s source this data from the enterprise. 
 PACComtrade database may include commodities that are not considered trade e.g., currency in circulation. As such the total value of trade for a period in the PACComtrade database may differ slightly from the IMTS’ total value of trade for the same period released by the countries.

fields.label: Data processing
fields.text: Commodity trade data processed by the Statistics for Development Division (SDD) of the Pacific Community (SPC) and published on the Pacific Data Hub .Stat statistical database under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Public License (CC-BY-4.0) (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/legalcode). The PACComtrade datasets are administrative statistics automatically generated from customs data. These datasets are updated monthly through an automated process. The system applies a series of validation rules to ensure data quality, including checks for the presence of mandatory fields and the validity of classification codes (e.g. country or commodity codes). Each time the process is executed, a validation report is produced, summarising any inconsistencies or erroneous entries. This report is shared with the relevant customs organisation for review and correction, if necessary. Technical documentation of the PACComtrade process can be found on the dedicated GitHub repository (https://github.com/PacificCommunity/PACComtrade).

fields.label: Additional comments
fields.text:
The following caveats with respect to the exhaustiveness applies to the PACComtrade database:
 
 PACComtrade database is a commodity trade database and not International Merchandise Trade Statistics (IMTS) i.e., these data sourced from Customs Administrations are used for compiling IMTS by National Statistics Offices (NSO) but are supplemented with data from other sources as well. For example, fuel sold to visiting aircraft, which is re-export, are not captured by quite a number of Customs administrations so the NSO’s source this data from the enterprise. 
 PACComtrade database may include commodities that are not considered trade e.g., currency in circulation. As such the total value of trade for a period in the PACComtrade database may differ slightly from the IMTS’ total value of trade for the same period released by the countries.

fields.text: Technology names are standardized by removing spaces, capitalizing words, and appending "(total)" where applicable. Grid connection categories are standardized ("All" becomes "Grid(total)"). The disaggregation variable is constructed by combining standardized technology and grid connection labels.

 Example :

fields.text: CC 3.0 IGO

fields.label: Additional comments
fields.text:
Reference model 
 (https://github.com/PacificCommunity/ofp-sam-yft-2023-diagnostic#reference-model) 
 In SPC assessment jargon, the diagnostic model is the reference model that is the basis of several sections and figures in the stock assessment report. 
 The diagnostic model is also the entry point when configuring and running the grid of ensemble models that is the basis of scientific advice. When the grid includes specific factor levels (for steepness, likelihood weights, etc.) the diagnostic model has intermediate levels, while other grid members explore higher and lower levels. 
 Finally, the diagnostic model is also the starting point for the stock assessment models development. One purpose of the SPC's GitHub repositories is to give the stock assessor a good starting point that is organized and documented.

fields.label: Comment
fields.text:
UN Tourism collects, standardizes and publishes statistics of tourism, and promotes the integration of these statistics within the sphere of the United Nations system. 
 Data are collected and updated on a regular basis through questionnaires to country statistical focal points. 
 The definitions and classifications used are based on the International Recommendations for Tourism Statistics 2008 (https://www.unwto.org/tourism-statistics/on-basic-tourism-statistics-irts-2008), approved by the United Nations Statistical Commission at its 39th session (26-29 February 2008). 
 NOTE: The results presented are based on a newly implemented data collection process, based on a new unified questionnaire. The corresponding new data processing system is currently in a transitional phase, and therefore some data points may not yet fully reflect the intended standards. We appreciate your understanding as we continue the ongoing improvements, which are also expected to gradually increase the completeness of the datasets.

fields.label: Data processing
fields.text: Data are filtered to SPC member countries and restricted to three disaggregation levels: total visitor arrivals, tourists, and excursionists.

fields.label: License
fields.text: CC-BY

fields.label: Additional comments
fields.text:
Data are sourced from UN Tourism. A tourist is defined as an overnight visitor staying at least one night in a collective or private accommodation in the country visited; same-day visitors are included in the total. Values represent absolute counts of arrivals. Tourism is sensitive to climate change, which can damage key assets such as coral reefs and beaches, increase extreme weather events, and ultimately reduce the attractiveness of destinations with significant economic consequences for Pacific island nations heavily reliant on tourism revenues. 
 Example : 
 In 1997, French Polynesia recorded a value of 201,000, indicating that 201,000 tourists arrived on this territory at that time. By 2022, the indicator for French Polynesia had reached 261,400, meaning that 261,400 tourists went there.

fields.label: Title of the dataset
fields.text: Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI)

fields.label: Source organisation
fields.text: World Bank (WB)

fields.label: Comment
fields.text: Governance—the traditions and institutions by which authority in a country is exercised—plays a central role in shaping development outcomes. A large body of research highlights how inclusive and accountable institutions support higher economic growth, stronger public services, and expanded opportunities. When governance systems struggle to perform these functions, development outcomes are often harder tosustain. First published in 1999, the Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) provide annual composite indicators summarizing six dimensions of governance: - Voice and Accountability – capturing perceptions of the extent to which citizens can participate in selecting their government, including electoral integrity, and perceptions of accountability mechanisms for citizens—reflected in the ability to access information, governmental oversight bodies, and a robust traditional/digital media landscape. - Political Stability – capturing perceptions of the extent to which political power and governance are secure from destabilization, and of the likelihood that authority will be challenged or altered through violent, coercive, or unconstitutional means. - Government Effectiveness – capturing perceptions of the quality of public services, the civil service, policy formulation and implementation, and the credibility of a government’s decisions. - Regulatory Quality – capturing perceptions of the government’s ability to design and implement policies and regulations that promote private sector development. - Rule of Law – capturing perceptions of the extent to which agents respect and follow the rules of society, including contract enforcement, property rights, the police, courts, and the likelihood of crime and violence. - Control of Corruption – capturing perceptions of the extent to which public power is used for private gain, including both petty and grand corruption, as well as capture of the state by elites and private interests.

fields.label: Data processing
fields.text: The WGI 2025 release included methodological revisions, and hence historical estimates have been recalculated back to 1996 to ensure full consistency over time. The WGI draw on perception data from 35 cross-country sources—including household surveys, firm surveys, and expert assessments—to offer a comparable picture of governance quality across more than 200 economies from 1996 to 2024. Each question or variable from the underlying data sources is mapped to up to two of the six governance dimensions. It is then rescaled to range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating better governance outcomes. When multiple questions or variables from the same source map to the same dimension, they are averaged so that each data source contributes only one signal per dimension. The rescaled data from the individual sources are combined using a weighted average—estimated through a statistical technique known as an Unobserved Components Model (UCM)—to construct each of the six WGI dimension estimates. The UCM weights reflect the pattern of correlations among the sources: sources that are more strongly correlated with each other receive more weight, while those that are less correlated receive less. This weighting improves the precision of the aggregate indicators. The WGI produces two outputs for each country, year, and governance dimension. First, the model yields a governance estimate, which is normally distributed with a mean near zero and typically ranges between –2.5 and 2.5, accompanied by its model-based standard error. Second, this estimate is mapped onto an absolute 0–100 scale, with corresponding 90-percent confidence intervals, to facilitate comparisons across countries and over time.

The findings, interpretations, and conclusions expressed in this work do not necessarily reflect the views of the World Bank, its Board of Executive Directors, or the governments they represent, nor do they constitute an official World Bank rating of the quality of governance in a particular country. The World Bank does not guarantee the accuracy, completeness, or currency of the data included in this work and does not assume responsibility for any errors, omissions, or discrepancies in the information, or liability with respect to the use of or failure to use the information, methods, processes, or conclusions set forth. Usage Advisory: This usage advisory aims to provide clarity on the limitations and appropriate use of the WGI data, ensuring that users are well-informed about the nature and scope of the indicators. 1. Amalgamation of Survey Data and Expert Assessments: The WGI are based on 35 data sources that fall into two broad categories: (1) surveys of households and firms (accounting for 14 data sources), and (2) expert assessments (accounting for 21 data sources). Household and firm surveys capture the views of people living and working in the countries to which the data apply. Expert assessments reflect the views and perceptions of experts employed and/or convened by the organizations producing the data sources. 2. WGI is Derived from Subjective Perceptions-Based Data: All the data used in the WGI is perceptionsbased and inherently subjective. The views and perceptions of firms, experts and households matter because they make decisions based on those views and perceptions. 3. Governance scores: Accordingly, the governance scores of countries in the WGI are intended to reflect general conclusions arising from the compilation of accumulated data, applying the methodology described. A country's scores may change from year to year because of variations in the underlying values in the source data, or in some cases, data availability. Scores are not intended to reflect a definitive statement or hierarchy of government performance or effectiveness. 4. Lag in Perception Changes: Perceptions may be slower to change than actual governance reforms. As a result, there may be a delay between changes in laws, rules, and their implementation in any country and the perceptions of those changes captured in survey data and expert assessments. 5. Intended Use of WGI: The WGI are intended for research and policy analysis purposes. WGI data are not intended to serve as definitive criteria for use in credit assessments, sovereign credit ratings, investment
